problems.description: create_task() replaces SQLite's atomic AUTOINCREMENT id with SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id)+1,0) followed by an explicit INSERT — a classic TOCTOU race. Two concurrent POSTs can compute the same next_id, one failing with an IntegrityError (500). This is a correctness regression in the core data path that static analysis (bugs +0) cannot detect.
init_db() now runs at module import time, introducing an import-time side effect: importing app.py creates the schema and fails hard if the DB file is unwritable, harming test isolation.
The zero-based id scheme adds manual bookkeeping with no functional payoff — INTEGER PRIMARY KEY already auto-assigns; the extra SELECT/INSERT pair is pure complexity.
Removing the '# ── Models ──' / '# ── Routes ──' section banners slightly reduces file navigability, though this is stylistic.

strengths: Fixes a real seed bug: tasks were created with status 'done'; the INSERT now defaults to 'pending'.
Adds robust request-body validation (isinstance dict + title type check) to POST/PUT, returning 400 instead of silently coercing.
Removes dead code (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin stub) matching the measured smell delta (-1).
Adds explicit conn.commit() after CREATE TABLE, making schema initialization deterministic.
Preserves existing helper signatures (fetch_task alias) and type-hinted function style, so the module shape stays intact.
commit_reviews.summary: Useful cleanup (bug-fixed status default, input validation, dead-code removal, -1 smell) but it introduces a latent concurrency bug via hand-rolled MAX(id)+1 id allocation that the SonarQube bugs +0 can't see, and its 0.70 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) rather than this diff.

problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled (base64url + hmac + exp/alg checks) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT; bespoke crypto is a common source of auth bypasses, and the SonarQube +25 cognitive complexity delta confirms the code is non-trivial enough to warrant a library.
JWT_SECRET falls back to the hard-coded 'development-secret-change-me' when the env var is unset, so any deployment without the env var has forgeable tokens.
decode_token's bare `except (ValueError, ..., Exception)` makes the enumerated exceptions redundant and silently masks coding errors.
Inconsistent datetime handling: deprecated naive `datetime.utcnow()` in create_task vs timezone-aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` in create_token.

Ownership scoping is threaded through the DB layer as an optional owner_id (None means unscoped), conflating 'unauthenticated' with 'admin/global'; policy enforcement belongs at the API layer and the visible diff doesn't demonstrate route-level protection for every mutation.
Tokens carry only sub/exp — no iat/jti, so there is no way to revoke a token or audit token issuance.

strengths: The `PRAGMA table_info` + nullable owner_id migration preserves existing tasks and is backward compatible.
The `authenticated` decorator with `g.current_user` is idiomatic Flask and cleanly separates auth from route logic.
Correct defensive choices: `hmac.compare_digest` for constant-time comparison and an explicit `alg == HS256` allowlist.
Post-INSERT SELECT returns the authoritative row rather than assembling a dict by hand.
commit_reviews.summary: A functional, backward-compatible auth + ownership layer that follows the codebase's plain-Flask/SQLite patterns, but the hand-rolled JWT with a hard-coded default secret is real security debt — and note the mechanical convention score (0.70, 9 violations) is dragged down mostly by pre-existing files outside this diff (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py), which my 0.65 does not punish this commit for.

problems.description: Notification dispatch logic is inlined in the edit_task route handler (fetch previous_task, compare status, enqueue), mixing queue concerns into the controller rather than a small service/domain layer; acceptable for this app size but couples the HTTP layer to the queueing contract.
TOCTOU race: previous_task is read before update_task, so two concurrent completion PUTs could both observe previous status != completed and enqueue duplicate notifications.
previous_task = get_task(...) adds an extra DB read on every edit request, including non-transition edits that never enqueue.

Default Celery broker/backend point at redis://localhost:6379/0 (DB 0), the same instance/db the story tests flushdb()/flushall() during testing; a separate DB number or queue-aware config would isolate broker state from test teardown.

strengths: Correct transition-only detection (previous != completed -> completed) with tests covering both the enqueue path and the no-duplicate re-completion path
Async side-effect cleanly decoupled via Celery .delay(); Celery() construction is lazy so app import does not break when Redis is unavailable
Follows existing app conventions: g.current_user, update_task/get_task reuse, snake_case functions, type hints, docstring on the task, and existing register/login/monkeypatch test helpers
Minimal, cohesive diff (+3 files, +56/-0) that adds the feature without restructuring
Tests assert on the queued payload, not just status code
commit_reviews.summary: A small, well-tested, pattern-respecting async notification feature whose only real blemishes are inlined queue logic in the controller, a theoretical double-enqueue race, and analyzer noise rather than genuine convention breaks.

problems.description: Repositories are instantiated per request (TaskRepository(DATABASE) / UserRepository(DATABASE) in every handler) instead of once and injected, so the pattern is applied but not wired cleanly.

Timestamp generation stays in the route layer: create_task() passes datetime.utcnow().isoformat() (deprecated in 3.12) into the repository, splitting persistence concerns awkwardly instead of letting the repository own record creation.
The extracted SQL layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository, ~174 new lines) ships with no new unit tests in this commit despite being a behavior-preserving refactor of critical code.

repositories.py carries one of the 9 flagged convention violations (module-level constant casing); the remaining 8 are in files untouched by this commit (app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py), so the 0.70 mechanical score overstates this commit's own lint debt.

strengths: Extracts ~76 lines of duplicated inline SQL into a reusable BaseRepository ABC with concrete TaskRepository/UserRepository, removing central duplication from app.py.
Preserves route-layer function signatures (create_task, get_tasks, get_task, update_task) and behaviors — bugs +0, smells +0, cognitive complexity -1, duplications 0.0% confirm no regression.
Idiomatic modern Python: ABC + abstractmethod, type hints on public signatures, sqlite3.Row factory reuse, context-managed connections — consistent with the repo's stated conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, low-risk repository-pattern refactor that centralizes SQLite persistence out of app.py with preserved behavior and reduced complexity; the 0.70 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing lint noise in untouched files, though per-call repository instantiation, caller-owned timestamps, and missing tests are minor polish gaps.

problems.description: The test fixture calls limiter.reset() and the new rate-limit tests issue 100+ requests each; with storage_uri hardcoded to redis://localhost:6379/1, the formerly-hermetic SQLite-only test suite now requires a live Redis server to pass (no in-memory/storage fallback).

GET /tasks response envelope changed from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} without versioning or a compatibility shim — a breaking contract change for any existing consumer outside this diff.
The owner_id=None branch in list_tasks_page is unreachable — the only caller passes g.current_user['id'] — duplicating list_tasks logic as dead code.
total is recomputed via a full COUNT(*) over the owner's rows on every page request, not just the first page.

Measured convention score 0.70 with 9 violations, but those live in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, notifications.py, pre-existing module constants); the commit's own additions are snake_case/PascalCase clean and add no new violations.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination on stable id-descending ordering — no offset drift under concurrent inserts.
Per-identity rate-limit keys (authenticated user_id, IP fallback) correctly scope limits for both /tasks and the brute-force-prone auth endpoint.
New tests cover pagination order, total, next_cursor, limit bounds, 429 + Retry-After, and auth-endpoint throttling; existing tests were updated consistently.
Cross-cutting rate limiting is placed at the app boundary via flask-limiter with headers_enabled, matching the session's stated purpose.
Query params validated with proper 400s and a bounded limit (1..100); limit+1 over-fetch cleanly detects has_next_page.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested addition of keyset pagination and per-identity rate limiting that respects the existing repository/route layering, though it couples the previously-hermetic test suite to a live Redis dependency and ships an unversioned breaking response-envelope change.

compounding_issues: Session 1's hand-rolled zero-based ID allocation (MAX(id)+1, dropping AUTOINCREMENT) became the API's identity scheme that Sessions 2-5 all had to preserve and re-implement; Session 4's refactor re-encoded it in TaskRepository and Session 5's pagination built its id-based cursor on it, silently switching list ordering from created_at DESC to id DESC.

Session 2's hand-rolled HMAC JWT (no PyJWT) with a bare except-Exception fallthrough is security-critical bespoke code that Session 5's rate-limit keying (rate_limit_key -> decode_token) still depends on.

Session 3's notification/email dispatch stayed inline in the app.py route handler while Session 4 extracted persistence into repositories, leaving a layering inconsistency (no service layer for cross-cutting logic).
Session 5 changed the GET /tasks response shape from a bare list to an envelope object {data, total, next_cursor} — a breaking API change introduced in the final session.
Repo hygiene wart: binary artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc and todos.db) were committed in Sessions 3-4.
key_decisions: Session 1: hand-rolled zero-based ID allocation (MAX(id)+1) instead of AUTOINCREMENT, plus module-load init_db() for WSGI compatibility — a bespoke identity scheme that persisted through every later session.

Session 2: hand-rolled HMAC-SHA256 JWT auth (no library) with per-user task ownership and in-place schema migration (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN owner_id) — the pivot from an anonymous single-file API to an authenticated multi-tenant one.
Session 3: async notification integration via Celery/Redis (notifications.py + celery_config.py), gated on a pending->completed status transition, adding a worker/Redis infrastructure dependency.
Session 4: repository-layer extraction (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository), cleaning the app.py monolith while preserving migrations.
Session 5: cross-cutting hardening — flask-limiter rate limiting keyed by JWT identity-or-IP and cursor-based pagination, with requirements.txt added and response envelope change.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 tightened the seed's validation and removed dead stubs; Session 2 added a real auth layer with tests and schema migration; Session 3 layered Celery notifications with transition-gated tests; Session 4 improved structure via the repository pattern; Session 5 rounded out production concerns with pagination and rate limiting, and the test suite grew at each step (test_app.py accumulating coverage for migration, ownership isolation, pagination bounds, and 429s). The gains came with mild local costs — a breaking response-shape change in the final session, an id-vs-created_at ordering drift, and a small leftover layering inconsistency around notifications — but the arc is a clear monotone improvement from throwaway script toward a structured, tested, multi-tenant API.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc (cleanup → auth → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) in which the agent both grew the feature surface and steadily raised structural and test quality, with only minor technical debt carried forward from early hand-rolled decisions.
